title: No blacks in the studio orchestras
summary: Carter kept his band for security because few blacks worked in film; only Lee Young held a studio contract.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: And you were not, though, saying to everybody, 'Look, I'm gonna get out of the band business and I'm gonna stay in Hollywood.' It didn't happen like that, did it?

No. I didn't see it happening like that because at that particular time, I mean, of course, I've never really assumed a defeatist attitude, and what I'm trying to say is that at that time, blacks were not really encouraged to feel that they would be in demand or ... oh, what's the word I want to use?
They were not encouraged to feel that people were going to be calling on them?

I guess -- I guess that's the feeling, you know; you wonder how much time can you put into this and what can you look forward to, you know, and as long as I had the band, I sort of felt that I should hold on to that for a little security, although I wanted to write for pictures, and at that time, there, -- gee, I don't think there were any other blacks that I knew of that had been working in film, other than Phil Bill Moore and Calvin Jackson, who had come to California with Harry James to work on a picture at MGM.
There were no blacks in the studio orchestras. You know.
Right. You got in to the studio orchestras. Did you get work in the studios as a conductor and so on around that time?

Yes. No, not as a conductor -- but I did do a bit of work as, you know, the player. I did a number of things as a player, and also as a player in the orchestra, and a player on screen with, you know, my own groups at different times.

But there were no blacks in the staff orchestras that were under contract. That's what I was trying to get to. And the only instance -- I know of one having been under contract was Lee Young, who is a percussionist and was with Columbia for some years, under contract. But of course, they don't have contract orchestras any more, but they did then. But they didn't have any blacks that I knew of, other than Lee Young.

Right. The existence, then, of this possibility of work in films embraced arranging in this early period -- arranging; the playing, with ... in the studio -- and at the same time, you had your band which was still touring. You were touring '43, '44, '45 -- and I -- around when do you recall was it that this band slid out of existence, so to speak?
Seems, it was about the end of '46,
